summary: A changing system of British colonies, protectorates, dominions and other dependencies, governed through different degrees of direct and indirect control.
currency: Pound sterling and numerous territorial currencies; imperial territories did not share one uniform monetary system.
rulers: Selected monarch: Victoria, 1837–1901; policy was also directed by ministers, Parliament and colonial administrations.
economy: Imperial commerce and colonial resources supported industrial growth; exploitation and coercion shaped the distribution of economic benefits.
military: British forces and colonial armies secured territories and trade routes; losing access to the Indian Army weakened Britain’s global military capacity after 1947.
origin: Merchant charters, Atlantic settlement and overseas conquest produced an expanding imperial system; Jamestown became a permanent English settlement in 1607.
decline: Independence movements and postwar political change dismantled most colonial rule; Hong Kong’s transfer to China in 1997 became a symbolic endpoint.
periodNote: 1607 begins this overseas-settlement convention; 1997 is a symbolic endpoint. Earlier English expansion preceded it, and British Overseas Territories remained afterward.
name: British Empire
identityNote: Same overseas imperial umbrella. AtlasPI starts with the 1583 Newfoundland claim; the dossier uses the 1607 Jamestown settlement convention. Both end symbolically with Hong Kong in 1997. Do not interpret either interval as dissolution of all dependencies.
